intro: Zoom for podcast producers on Mac is a remote recording room. Guests join by link, and the Zoom desktop app can save each person's audio as its own file. Those separate files are what you edit in Descript, Audacity, or Adobe Audition.
tldr: Turn on local recording and the separate audio file setting on the host Mac and on every guest Mac. Everyone needs the desktop app.
The separate audio setting is easy to miss. Check it before the call, not after the first recording lands in your folder.
Recording Studio gives isolated video per guest, but it needs a Zoom Events or Webinars Plus license on top of your plan.
Ask Lazur to point at the Allow Record option or walk you through the settings, one click at a time.

blocks.text: Most podcast producers use Zoom on a Mac as a remote recording room. You send a link, guests join, and the desktop app saves each person on their own file. That is the core of it. Everything else is settings, file handling, and a few traps that catch people in their first season.
Why producers use Zoom to record remote episodes

Zoom's podcasting page says it can record each speaker on their own audio track for clean editing. It promotes local recording, noise cancellation, and integrations with Descript, Audacity, and Adobe Audition. It does not list podcast templates or a built-in editor. Zoom records the conversation. Your editing app does the rest.

A Castos survey of 99 podcast creators, published May 28, 2026, found that remote platforms were the most common setup. Zoom was one of them. The survey gives no Zoom-only numbers, so it shows habit, not how well Zoom works for you. Treat it as context, not proof.

Most creators in that survey do not record video. Their audio-only sessions depend most on clean separate tracks. Without a camera angle, a bad take on one microphone is hard to hide. Separate files give you a second chance at the edit.
Set up separate audio files in Zoom on Mac
Set up the host Mac before anyone joins. The steps below come from Macworld and Glenn Fleishman's 2021 walkthrough. Menu labels differ by version, so match the meaning to what you see on your screen.

items: Update the Zoom desktop app. Zoom renamed it Zoom Workplace in April 2024. Releasebot lists macOS 7.2.5 dated Oct 31, 2026, but this guide could not match that to Zoom's own release notes, so check your version.
Turn on local recording for your account. The web portal setting reads 'Hosts can give meeting participants permission to record locally', according to Fleishman's walkthrough.

Open zoom.us > Preferences > Recording in the app. Tick the separate audio option. Macworld calls it 'Create separate audio files for each participant'. Fleishman calls it 'Record a separate audio file for each participant'.
If you edit video in another app, also tick 'Optimize for 3rd party video editor'. Macworld says to check it when editing video.
Run a short test with one other Mac. Stop the test, open the recording folder, and count the files before the real call.

blocks.text: The file count is your proof. You want one file for you and one file for each guest. If you see a single file that holds both voices, the setting was off when you pressed record. Fix it, then test again. Do not assume the next recording will be different.
Get every guest on the Zoom desktop app

Every guest on a Mac needs the Zoom desktop app. Browser and mobile Zoom cannot record locally, according to Fleishman's account. A guest who joins from a browser tab cannot give you a local track, no matter what you set on your side.

Send guests the steps before the call, not during it. The path in Fleishman's setup is profile icon > Settings > Recording tab. Guests tick the separate audio option, then send you their audio file after the call.

items: Open the Zoom desktop app and sign in.
Click your profile icon, then choose Settings.
Open the Recording tab and tick 'Record a separate audio file for each participant'.
After the call, find the Audio Record subfolder and send the audio file to the host.

blocks.text: Give your guest permission to record locally

Sometimes the host has to allow a participant to record. Hover over the name in the Participants list, click More, and select Allow Record. Macworld describes this path. Zoom then notifies everyone when recording starts and asks each person to acknowledge it.

Plan for that notice. Tell guests it will appear, so they know it is expected. Ask them to confirm it before you start talking. A quick heads-up saves you from explaining a pop-up in the middle of an answer.

blocks.text: Local recording is the setup most podcast producers use. Each Mac saves its own files on its own disk. The host gets the host's file right away. Each guest's file stays on the guest's Mac until they send it to you.

Cloud recording works differently. It keeps a copy in Zoom's cloud and counts against storage. Zoom's pricing page lists local recording for Basic. Check the page before you choose a plan, because cloud storage limits decide how many episodes fit.
Find your local recordings and clean up the extras

Macworld says local recordings default to a Zoom folder in Documents. Each recording goes into a subfolder named with its start date and time. When the meeting ends, Zoom converts the files and opens the folder in the Finder. You can stop the conversion and resume it later.

Zoom cannot skip video for local recordings. Fleishman reports deleting unwanted video files by hand. Look inside each folder before you move anything, and keep the audio files you need. Video you do not want can still take up space.

blocks.title: Check the menus on your Mac
blocks.text: Sources in this guide disagree on the path to the recording setting, and the Mac steps come from 2021 and 2022 writing. Zoom's own Mac support page for separate audio was not checked. Confirm each menu path before you rely on it for a paid session.
Mistakes that cost podcast producers an episode

items: Checking the setting after the call. Fleishman found the right settings only after the session ended. The first recording was one composite of both speakers.
Trusting a browser guest. Browser and mobile Zoom cannot record locally, so you get no local track from them.
Forgetting the send step. A guest's audio file stays on their Mac until they send it to you.
Testing the microphone only in QuickTime. One guest's employer-issued Mac blocked USB microphone selection there. Zoom's local recording worked with their USB mic.
Moving files during conversion. Conversion can be interrupted and resumed. Wait for the folder to finish before you move anything.
Running out of cloud space. Pro and Business include 10 GB per license. Recording Studio files run about 2 to 3 GB per hour at 1080p60.

blocks.text: Recording Studio: when the extra license is worth it

Recording Studio is Zoom's option for isolated video per guest. Zoom says it delivers edit-ready files organized by speaker and take. If you record video for every episode, it may matter. If you record audio only, you probably do not need it.

The limits are strict. It works only for single-session meetings created in Zoom Webinars Plus and Events. Webinar event types are not supported. Screen shares land in the cloud recording only, not in the local files. Zoom's support article caps it at 10 participants recorded at once and 10 takes per session.

The licensing is layered. The support article lists a Pro, Business, Enterprise, or Education account. It also needs a Zoom Events Unlimited or Pay Per Attendee license, or a Webinars Plus equivalent, and cloud recording on. Zoom's pricing page does not mention Recording Studio, so check their pricing page before you buy anything.

On a Mac, Zoom says Recording Studio needs Apple silicon, M1 or later, with an 8-core or higher CPU. The same article gives a desktop version of 6.7.0 or higher in one place and 7.0 or later in another. It does not reconcile the two. If you use it, install 7.0 or later.
Storage and file size for a season of episodes

Recording Studio files run about 2 to 3 GB per hour at 1080p60. Zoom recommends at least 30 GB of cloud recording storage, and 200 GB or more for frequent users. Check your storage before a season starts, not when the first upload fails.

Local audio files are not in that table. Zoom's notes do not give a size for them. Measure one test file yourself. Open the folder, check the file size of a short recording, and scale it to your episode length.
Where Lazur fits in a Zoom session

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ (hold Option + Command) to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It does not click buttons for you. You still make each change in Zoom.

Use it for the questions that come up during setup. Ask where a control is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to change a setting, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Ask during the call, not after. Ask where Allow Record is while the guest waits. Ask it to explain a notice that covers your view. Keep the answers short, and confirm them against the menu on your screen.

Lazur also covers the work around the recording. Set a timer for the segment. Add an Apple Reminders item for the guest's file. Hold fn to dictate a timestamp note, and the text types at the cursor in any app.

Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur is not a Zoom add-in, and it has no partnership with Zoom.
Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, not available. You can get it from the [download page](/download).
A worked example from setup to finished files

Start before the guest arrives. Open the Zoom desktop app and check the version. Confirm local recording and the separate audio setting are on. Send your guest the short steps from earlier in this guide, so they set theirs before they join.

Start the meeting in the desktop app, not a browser tab. When the guest joins, hover over their name, click More, and select Allow Record if they need to record too. Start your local recording. Zoom shows the notice to everyone, so wait for acknowledgments.

At the end, stop the recording and let Zoom finish converting. Open the Zoom folder in Documents. Find the subfolder with today's start time, and check that you have your own audio file. If the guest's file has not arrived, message them to send it.

Keep call notes in a text file next to the recordings. Note the start of each segment and any takes that went wrong. Editing goes faster when you know which take to keep. Dictate the notes with fn so you can keep your eyes on the call.
Next steps for your next episode

items: Run a short test with one other Mac and check both files.
Save the guest steps as a message you send before every call.
Check Recording Studio only if you need isolated video for each guest.
Check your cloud storage against your episode plan before a season starts.
Ask Lazur to point at Allow Record when you need it.

blocks.text: Start with the test. A bad file in episode one costs more than a short test call. Once the test passes, the rest of the season runs on the same settings.

faq.question: Can I record separate audio tracks in Zoom on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Turn on local recording and the separate audio setting, then have each guest do the same in the Zoom desktop app. Macworld calls the setting useful for podcast editing. Each guest's file stays on their Mac until they send it to you.

faq.question: Do guests need the Zoom desktop app on a Mac too?
faq.answer: For a local track, yes. Browser and mobile Zoom cannot record locally, so the guest needs the desktop app. Their audio then saves as a separate file on their own Mac.

faq.question: Where does Zoom save local recordings on a Mac?
faq.answer: Macworld says the default is a Zoom folder in Documents. Each recording gets a subfolder named with its start date and time. After the call, Zoom converts the files and opens the folder in the Finder.

faq.question: Is Recording Studio the same as separate audio files?
faq.answer: No. Separate audio files are a local recording setting. Recording Studio captures isolated local video for each guest. It needs a Zoom Events or Webinars Plus license and cloud recording turned on.

faq.question: Why did my Zoom recording come out as one file for both speakers?
faq.answer: The separate audio setting was probably off. Glenn Fleishman's 2021 podcast setup produced one composite file first, and the right settings were found only after the session. Check the setting before every call.

faq.question: How much cloud storage do I need for podcast recordings?
faq.answer: Zoom's pricing page lists 10 GB of cloud storage per license on Pro and Business. Zoom recommends at least 30 GB of cloud recording storage for Recording Studio files, and 200 GB or more for frequent users.

faq.question: Can Lazur record my Zoom call for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur answers questions, points at controls, and guides you one click at a time. It does not click buttons or operate Zoom for you. You still start and stop recording yourself.
